subject: Critical Thinking
title: Utilitarianism: The Greatest Good for the Greatest Number
description: A quick, practical guide to Utilitarianism: The Greatest Good for the Greatest Number.

hook.text: A city needs a hospital or a concert hall. The hospital saves lives. The concert hall brings joy to thousands.

buildup.text: Jeremy Bentham: the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number.

twist.text: The dark side: utilitarianism can justify sacrificing one person to save five.

climax.text: Every policy decision – healthcare allocation, tax policy, environmental law – implicitly uses utilitarian reasoning.

punchline.text: Utilitarianism sounds simple until every gain must be weighed against every sacrifice.

quiz.question: What is the core principle of utilitarianism?
options: The right action produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number

details.summary: Utilitarianism judges actions solely by their outcomes, aiming to maximize total happiness or well-being for the greatest number of people. It strips moral evaluation down to a simple calculus of consequences.
details.whyItMatters: Utilitarian thinking underpins public policy, healthcare triage, and everyday trade-offs whenever resources are scarce.
takeaways: Actions are right if they produce the most overall good
Pleasure and pain are the core utilitarian metrics
Critics argue it can justify harming individuals for the majority

faq.question: What is the main idea behind utilitarianism?
faq.answer: The right action is the one that produces the greatest net happiness across all affected parties. Everything else—intentions, duties—is secondary to outcomes.

faq.question: What is a common criticism of utilitarian reasoning?
faq.answer: It can justify sacrificing one innocent person if doing so makes the majority happier, which conflicts with strong moral intuitions about individual rights.
